1191.quote_or_event: “She alone is the happy soul-bride, who is pleasing to God.”
1191.explanation: Guru Arjan says that the true sohagan, the fortunate wedded soul-bride, is the one her Lord loves in return.
1191.tie_back: The Kural says that those loved back by the one they love have won love's stoneless fruit; Gurbani likewise names the soul-bride who pleases her Beloved as the truly blessed one.
1191.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 391, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1191._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on the blessing of being loved by the one you love, though the love is spiritual, between the soul and God, and Gurbani has no stoneless-fruit image.

1192.quote_or_event: “Just as the earth looks beautiful when the rain falls, so does the Sikh blossom forth meeting the Guru.”
1192.explanation: Guru Ram Das compares the Sikh's joy on meeting the Guru to the dry earth turning green and beautiful under rain.
1192.tie_back: The Kural says a lover's kindness to the one who loves him is like rain to those whose life depends on it; Gurbani uses the same rain image for the Guru's grace to the longing Sikh.
1192.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 758, Raag Soohee, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1192._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit, with the same rain-on-the-earth image for welcome grace, though the giver is the Guru and the relationship is spiritual, not that of lovers.

1193.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, the soul-bride is forever the Lord's favorite wife; her Husband Lord does not die, and He shall never leave.”
1193.explanation: Guru Amar Das says the soul-bride who is truly loved by the Lord is sure of her happiness, because her Husband never dies and never leaves her.
1193.tie_back: The Kural says only a woman loved by the one she loves can say with proud confidence, 'We shall live happily yet'; Gurbani gives the loved soul-bride the same sure confidence, since her Beloved will never leave.
1193.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 245, Raag Gauree, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1193._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on the loved bride's confidence that her happiness is secure, though Gurbani grounds it in an undying divine Husband, not a husband who will come home from a journey.

1194.quote_or_event: “Without the Name of the Lord, the beautiful are just like the noseless ones.”
1194.explanation: Guru Ram Das says that beauty and the admiration it wins mean nothing without love for the Lord's Name; such a person is as disgraced as one whose nose has been cut off.
1194.tie_back: The Kural says that even a woman everyone admires is unfortunate if the one she loves does not love her back; Gurbani likewise says the admired and beautiful are without real worth if they lack the love that matters.
1194.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 528, Raag Dayv Gandhaaree, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1194._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable fit on admired beauty that counts for nothing without the one bond that matters, but Gurbani's lack is the Name, not a lover's love in return.

1195.quote_or_event: “But one who feels good only when good is done for him, and feels bad when things go badly - do not call him a lover. He trades only for his own account.”
1195.explanation: In Asa di Vaar, Guru Angad says that love which asks what it will get, and sours when it gets nothing, is not love but trading.
1195.tie_back: The Kural's wife asks what good her beloved can do her if he does not love her back; Guru Angad answers that real love does not ask what it gains, so the verse is a gentle Sikh counterpoint to her complaint.
1195.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa, Asa di Vaar, Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1195._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa), two consecutive lines of one salok; next-best match and partly a contrast: both weigh love against what it returns, but the Kural voices a hurt lover's complaint while Guru Angad condemns love that keeps accounts.

1196.quote_or_event: “O Lord, if You will not break with me, then I will not break with You.”
1196.explanation: Bhagat Ravidas describes his love for God as a two-way bond, kept whole because neither side breaks it.
1196.tie_back: The Kural says love is painful when it rests on one end only and sweet, like a balanced carrying-pole, when it rests on both; Ravidas likewise sees true love as a bond held up from both sides.
1196.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 658, Raag Sorath, Bhagat Ravidas (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1196._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong thematic fit on love as a two-sided bond, though it has no carrying-pole image and the relationship is between the devotee and God.

1197.quote_or_event: “O sexual desire, you lead the mortals to hell; you make them wander in reincarnation through countless species.”
1197.explanation: In the Saloks Sehskritee, Guru Arjan addresses kaam (lust), one of the five thieves, as a force that drags people into suffering and rebirth.
1197.tie_back: The Kural's wife complains that Kama, the god of love, works only on her and ignores her pain; Gurbani also speaks to desire directly, but treats it as a thief to be overcome, not a god to be pleaded with.
1197.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1358, Saloks Sehskritee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1197._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); weak, next-best match offered as an honest contrast: both speak to desire as a power that causes suffering, but Sikhism does not worship a love-god, and it ranks kaam among the five thieves, while the Kural's Kama is a conventional poetic deity of married love.

1198.quote_or_event: “Many talk of the pain and suffering of separation; O pain, you are the ruler of all. Fareed, that body, within which love of the Lord does not well up - look upon that body as a cremation ground.”
1198.explanation: Sheikh Farid calls the pain of separation the ruler of all and says that a body which can live untouched by longing for the Beloved is no better than a cremation ground.
1198.tie_back: The Kural's wife says that anyone who goes on living without even one kind word from the beloved must be the hardest of hearts; Farid likewise sees a life untouched by longing for the Beloved as already dead.
1198.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 36) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1198._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa), both lines of salok 36; reasonable but partial fit: both judge the heart that endures life apart from the beloved, though the Kural is ironic self-reproach and Farid makes longing for God a mark of being truly alive.

1199.quote_or_event: “Continually listening to Your Glory, I live.”
1199.explanation: Guru Arjan says that hearing about the Lord's glory is what keeps him alive.
1199.tie_back: The Kural's wife says that even if her beloved shows her no kindness, every word about him is sweet to her ears; Guru Arjan likewise lives on simply hearing the Beloved's praise.
1199.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 388, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1199._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on finding life in merely hearing of the beloved, even matching the commentators' reading of the Kural's 'icai' as fame or praise, though Gurbani never suggests the Lord withholds grace and the love is spiritual.

1200.quote_or_event: “Tell your troubles to the One who is the Source of all comfort.”
1200.explanation: Guru Nanak advises taking one's sorrows only to the Lord, who alone can relieve them.
1200.tie_back: The Kural's heart is mocked for telling its great pain to one who does not care, like trying to fill the sea; Guru Nanak points to where pain should be told: to the One who holds all comfort.
1200.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 16, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1200._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable fit as the positive side of the Kural's warning against telling one's pain to the indifferent, though it has no sea image and no address to one's own heart.
